q: Which of the following groups consists entirely of operators that C++ never permits any class to overload, however the class is written?
exp: The dot, pointer-to-member, scope-resolution, conditional and sizeof operators are fixed by the core language grammar itself and never route through operator-function lookup, so no class can redefine them (typeid is excluded for the same reason). A is the trap: new, delete, new[] and delete[] are among the operators a class explicitly can overload, to control its own memory allocation. C and D both name operators that can be overloaded — and C's members are a different kind of limitation, not a ban: overloading && , || or the comma operator costs their built-in short-circuit and sequencing guarantees, though unary ! has no such guarantee to lose in the first place.
reviewFix: Explanation narrowed. The key was right, but the rebuttal of group C asserted that it 'loses special evaluation-order behaviour when overloaded' as a property of all four operators listed. That holds for &&, || and the comma operator, which have built-in short-circuit or sequencing guarantees that vanish once overloaded, but not for unary !, which takes a single operand and has no such guarantee to begin with. The claim is now scoped to the three operators it is true of. Key B unchanged.

q: A class Flag overloads operator&& as a member function, so that a && b for two Flag objects calls that function. Which behaviour of the built-in && is lost as a result?

opts.A: Nothing is lost; the compiler still special-cases && so the second operand is skipped whenever overloading makes the first operand false
opts.B: The result type changes from bool to Flag, so && can no longer appear inside an if condition
opts.C: Overloading operator&& is rejected by the compiler, because && can never be given a class-type overload
opts.D: Short-circuit evaluation: the overload is an ordinary function call, so both arguments are evaluated with no guarantee that b is skipped when a is false

exp: Once operator&& is overloaded it is an ordinary function call, and C++ gives function arguments no evaluation-order or skip guarantee, so both a and b are evaluated even when a is false; the same loss of special behaviour applies to an overloaded || or comma operator. A is wrong because the built-in short-circuit special-casing applies only to the primitive-type form of &&, never to an overload. B and C invent effects (a changed result type, a rejected declaration) that the standard does not impose — a class-type && is legal, it is just no longer short-circuiting.

q: Overload resolution, overriding and hiding are three distinct mechanisms in C++ that are often confused with one another. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?

opts.A: Overload resolution picks among same-named functions with different parameter lists at compile time from the static types of the arguments; overriding replaces a virtual function's behaviour in a derived class for a matching signature and is dispatched at run time through the object's dynamic type; hiding occurs when a derived class declares a name that makes every base-class function of that name in that scope invisible to ordinary unqualified lookup, whether or not the signatures or virtual-ness match
opts.B: Overload resolution and overriding are the same mechanism applied respectively to non-virtual and virtual functions, while hiding is a compiler error that always stops the program from compiling
opts.C: Overriding is decided at compile time from the static type of the pointer or reference used to call it, while overload resolution and hiding both happen only at run time
opts.D: Hiding only happens when a derived class redeclares a function with a signature identical to a base class virtual function, which is also exactly what overriding requires

exp: The three operate on different axes — parameter-list matching at compile time for overload resolution, dynamic-type dispatch at run time for overriding, and plain name lookup (ignoring signature and virtual-ness) for hiding — and A states all three correctly. B wrongly collapses overriding into overload resolution and mischaracterises hiding as always an error, when unrelated base and derived overloads coexisting is perfectly legal C++ (just inconvenient). C reverses overriding's actual run-time dispatch. D is backwards: a matching signature on a virtual function is precisely what turns a would-be hiding declaration into an override instead of hiding it.

opts.A: It compiles, and save(5) calls whichever definition appears first in the class; the second definition is silently ignored
opts.B: It compiles and forms a valid overload pair, with the const version selected only when save is called through a const object
opts.C: It fails to compile: a top-level const on a pass-by-value parameter is not part of the function's parameter-type list, so both lines declare the exact same function, and giving that one function two separate bodies is a redefinition error
opts.D: It compiles, but calling save(5) is ambiguous and must be disambiguated with an explicit cast

exp: A const on a by-value parameter only stops the function body from reassigning its own local copy; it is invisible to callers and plays no part in the function's type, so int x and const int x describe one function, not two, and defining it twice is a redefinition error. B is the tempting mistake — const genuinely does distinguish overloads for a reference or pointer parameter (const T& versus T&), but never for a plain by-value one.

q: A Meters class has a non-explicit converting constructor from int and needs to support both m + 5 and 5 + m. operator+ is currently a member function, Meters operator+(const Meters& other) const. Why does this signature fail for 5 + m, and what is the fix?

opts.A: Nothing needs to change: the compiler automatically retries the reversed order on a member operator+ whenever the forward order fails to compile
opts.B: A member operator function's left operand is always the object it is called through, so 5 + m would require int to have a member operator+; making operator+ a free function, Meters operator+(const Meters&, const Meters&), lets the converting constructor apply to either argument and satisfies both orders
opts.C: The member function must instead be declared static, so that it no longer has an implicit first argument
opts.D: The fix is to add a second member overload, Meters operator+(int) const, inside the same class; that alone makes 5 + m compile

exp: m.operator+(5) works for m + 5 because a member operator's left operand is fixed to the object it is invoked on, but there is no way to write 5.operator+(m) since int has no members — so 5 + m can only compile if operator+ is a free function, letting overload resolution apply Meters's converting constructor to whichever argument needs it. D fails because an added member operator+(int) still only fixes the m + 5 order; it does nothing for 5 + m, where m is not the left operand.

q: A Vector class defines Vector& operator+=(const Vector& rhs); as a member function and wants to implement operator+ in terms of it, without duplicating the addition logic. Which is the canonical way to define operator+ so that a + b leaves both a and b unchanged?

opts.A: Vector& operator+(const Vector& rhs) { *this += rhs; return *this; } written as a member function, so that a + b mutates a and returns a reference to it
opts.B: Vector& operator+(const Vector& lhs, const Vector& rhs) { lhs += rhs; return lhs; }, mutating and returning the caller's own lhs object directly
opts.C: Vector operator+(const Vector& lhs, const Vector& rhs) { return lhs += rhs; }, calling operator+= directly through the const reference
opts.D: Vector operator+(Vector lhs, const Vector& rhs) { lhs += rhs; return lhs; }, taking the left operand by value so it becomes a modifiable local copy that operator+= mutates and the function returns

exp: Taking the left-hand operand by value gives the function its own private copy, so lhs += rhs mutates only that copy, which is then returned; the caller's original a and b are untouched, exactly matching the value semantics expected of +. A is the classic bug hiding in plain sight: a member operator+ written as *this += rhs; return *this; silently mutates the left-hand operand of a + b, which no caller expects from +. B and C both try to call the non-const operator+= through a const Vector& parameter, which does not compile.
